name: Design an Online Game Matchmaking Service
intent: Put players with similar skill and a good connection into the same match within seconds, then hand them a game server, for a million players online at once.
codeTitle: a matchmaking queue with widening search windows
finalIntro: A party of two joins a ranked queue and lands on a game server.
prompt: Design the matchmaking service for an online team game with a million players online at the peak. Players press Play alone or with friends, and want a fair match, a low ping (a short delay to the game server) and a short wait. When a match is found, a game server must be ready for it.
functional: Join a queue for a game mode, alone or as a party, and leave it again
Rate every player's skill and update the rating after each match
Find a match of balanced teams from players with similar ratings
Prefer players in the same region and keep ping low
Start a game server for the match and send every player its address
nonFunctional: Most players find a match within 30 seconds, and the rest within 90
Match quality is stated as a number, such as the rating gap or the win probability, so it can be tuned
Handle about 700 queue tickets per second and 70 new matches per second at the peak
Never put one player into two matches, and never lose a match once it is formed
A crashed matchmaker or a region that is down delays matches but does not cancel them
Resist smurfs (experts on new accounts), queue dodging (leaving when the match looks bad) and rating manipulation

firstAttempt.text: One database table is the queue. When a player presses Play, a row is added. A loop takes the two oldest rows, creates a match, and asks a single game server process to start it. Skill is ignored, and everyone is in the same queue.
limits: Strong and weak players meet, so one side is bored and the other is crushed
Players from different continents are matched and the ping is terrible for half of them
A friend group cannot queue together, and a party of five has no way to join a team of five
There is no way to trade fairness against waiting, so quiet hours either stall or give bad games
One loop and one table are a bottleneck, and one game server cannot run thousands of matches

steps.title: Rate skill and match within a window
steps.problem: Pairing the two oldest players ignores skill, so many games are one-sided, and the players on the weak side quit.
steps.fix: Give every player a rating that estimates their skill, such as Elo, Glicko or TrueSkill, which also keeps an uncertainty so that new players move quickly. A ticket holds the rating and the time it was created. The matchmaker looks for the waiting player whose rating is closest, and accepts the pair only if the gap fits inside a search window around each player. The window starts narrow, so early matches are fair, and widens with every second waited, up to a cap, so nobody waits for ever. A pair needs the gap to fit in both windows, which stops a long-waiting player from being matched against someone who has just arrived and would have refused.
steps.tradeoff: Fairness becomes a number that can be tuned, and a wait has a ceiling. Every widening step trades a little quality for speed, a rating is only an estimate, and the right start, speed and cap differ for each mode and each hour of the day.

steps.title: Split the queues by mode and region, and measure ping
steps.problem: A player in Sydney matched with a player in Frankfurt has a ping of 280 ms, and ranked and casual players have different rules.
steps.fix: Each combination of game mode and region has its own queue. When the client starts, it measures the round trip time to each region's ping endpoint, and the ticket carries the list of regions where the ping is acceptable, best first. The ticket is placed in the best region's queue, and as the wait grows it is also visible in the next best regions, so the ping limit widens together with the rating window. Within a match the server region is picked to give the lowest worst-case ping for all of its players, not the lowest average.
steps.tradeoff: Pings stay low and each queue is a small independent problem that can run on its own machine. Small queues are thin at night or in a small region, so the widening rules matter most there, and the ticket must be removed from every queue the moment it is matched in one of them.

steps.title: Queue parties as one ticket and balance the teams
steps.problem: Friends want to play together, and a party of five with mixed ratings does not fit into a pair-by-pair search.
steps.fix: A party service holds the group, and the party leader submits one ticket for all of them. The ticket's rating is based on the strongest member plus a penalty for the spread, because a party coordinates better than five strangers of the same average. Matching then fills two teams from tickets of different sizes, like putting a party of 3, a party of 2 and singles together, and picks the split with the closest sums of ratings. All the members are queued, matched and removed as a unit, and the ping limit is the worst ping among them.
steps.tradeoff: Friends can play together and the teams are balanced on the total. A party ticket is harder to match and waits longer, a small group playing against a group of strangers has an advantage that the rating penalty only estimates, and the whole party is lost if one member disconnects, so the ticket needs a heartbeat.

steps.title: Allocate a game server for each match
steps.problem: A formed match is useless until a server is ready, and starting a server from nothing takes tens of seconds.
steps.fix: When a match is formed, an allocator asks the fleet manager for a slot in the best region. Servers are containers started ahead of time and kept in a warm pool, so a slot is claimed in milliseconds. One server process runs a few matches, a claim is a single atomic write so that two matches never take the same slot, and the allocator sends the address and a one-time token to every player in the match. The warm pool is sized to the surge of matches that can start before a new server finishes starting, and an autoscaler grows it ahead of the evening peak.
steps.tradeoff: Matches start immediately and the fleet follows demand. A warm pool is paid for while it is idle, a failed allocation means the whole match has to be put back or placed in another region, and a surge bigger than the pool still causes a short stall.

steps.title: Tune quality against wait with data
steps.problem: A window that widens too fast gives lopsided games, and one that widens too slowly loses players in the queue, and nobody knows which is true on a given night.
steps.fix: Every match records the wait time of each player and a quality score, such as the rating gap and the predicted win probability, and the results after the game show whether the prediction was right. A metrics pipeline turns these into dashboards by mode, region and hour: median and 95th percentile wait, share of lopsided games, and share of players who left the queue. The widening speed and the cap are settings read by the matchmaker, changed gradually and compared between groups of players. Ratings are updated after each match from the result, and the update is applied once even if the result arrives twice.
steps.tradeoff: The balance is chosen from measurements, so it can change with the hour and the size of the crowd. It needs enough data per queue to be meaningful, small queues are noisy, and any change to the rules moves the whole rating system, so changes roll out slowly.

steps.title: Scale the matchmaker by owning queues
steps.problem: One matchmaker process handles the queues of the whole world, so it is a bottleneck at the peak and a single point of failure.
steps.fix: Each queue is owned by exactly one matchmaker shard at a time, and ownership is a lease (a time-limited claim that must be renewed) kept in a small consistent store, with a fencing token so that an old owner that paused cannot form a match after losing its lease. A shard keeps its queues in memory, sorted by rating, so a new ticket finds its neighbours without scanning everyone. The ticket is also written to a durable log. If a shard dies, another takes over the lease and rebuilds the queue from the log in seconds. Queues that are too busy are split by rating band, with an overlap so that players at the boundary are not stranded.
steps.tradeoff: Matching scales with the number of shards and survives the loss of one. Each queue is still a single writer, so a very hot queue needs splitting, the overlap between bands must be handled carefully to avoid placing a player twice, and a failover delays that queue for a few seconds.

failures.scenario: A matchmaker shard crashes with thousands of tickets in memory
failures.impact: Those players are stuck in a queue that nobody is serving, and a revived old process might still try to form matches.
failures.answer: The lease expires and another shard takes the queue over. It replays the ticket log to rebuild the queue, keeping each ticket's original time so nobody loses their place. The fencing token on every match makes the allocator and the rating store reject anything from the old owner.

failures.scenario: A region goes down in the evening peak
failures.impact: Its players cannot be matched, and the neighbouring regions receive a sudden flood of tickets with high ping.
failures.answer: Health checks mark the region as unavailable, and tickets are moved to the nearest regions with a higher ping limit. The extra load is absorbed by the warm pools and by the autoscaler. A banner tells players that the ping may be higher, and tickets are not accepted beyond what the surviving regions can serve.

failures.scenario: A player is placed in two matches at once
failures.impact: The player is in a game they cannot join and the other nine players wait for them.
failures.answer: A ticket has one state, and moving it from waiting to matched is a single conditional write, so only one matcher wins. Matches formed in overlapping queues commit the tickets they use together, and a match that loses any ticket is returned to the queue without penalty. A player who already has a live match is rejected when they try to queue again.

failures.scenario: No game server is ready when a match forms
failures.impact: Ten players have been waiting for a match and are now stuck at a loading screen.
failures.answer: The allocator tries the next best region and then the warm pool of a larger server type, with a short deadline. If nothing is available, the match goes back to the front of its queue with its original times, and an alert warns the on-call engineer that the warm pool is too small. Players can see a clear status rather than a frozen screen.

failures.scenario: An experienced player makes a new account to play against beginners
failures.impact: The smurf wins every game, and the beginners on the other team quit.
failures.answer: A new account has a high rating uncertainty, so the rating moves very fast after a few wins and the player is placed with equals quickly. Signals such as win rate, accuracy and device links raise the account's rating faster or flag it for review. Because the rating is a probability estimate, the fix is mostly speed of correction, not punishment.

alternatives.title: How to search for a match

options.name: Pair the longest-waiting player with the closest rating
options.pro: Simple, fair to the waiting, and easy to reason about
options.con: Greedy, so it can leave a poor pair when a better global arrangement exists

options.name: Collect tickets for a few seconds and match them in batches
options.pro: Better overall quality, since the algorithm sees many options at once
options.con: Adds a fixed delay to every player, and the batch size is another setting

options.name: Ask for a lobby and let players pick or invite
options.con: Slow, unbalanced and not fair to new players

alternatives.pick: Greedy with widening windows for small queues, and short batches of a second or two for the busiest ones.

alternatives.title: How the rating is calculated

options.name: Elo
options.pro: Very simple, one number, and easy to explain
options.con: No uncertainty, so new players take long to find their level, and it is built for one-against-one

options.name: Glicko
options.pro: Adds a rating deviation, so uncertain players move faster
options.con: Still a one-against-one model, and teams need an extension

options.name: TrueSkill
options.pro: Designed for teams and several teams, and it tracks uncertainty
options.con: More complex maths, and harder to tune and explain to players

alternatives.pick: A model with uncertainty, such as Glicko or TrueSkill, because new accounts and teams are the common case.

alternatives.title: How the queue is stored

options.name: A database table
options.pro: Durable and simple, and fine for a small game
options.con: Polling a table at this rate is slow and contended

options.name: In memory in the owning shard, with a log for recovery
options.pro: Fast sorted search and cheap updates
options.con: Needs leases and a replay to recover

options.name: A shared sorted set in a cache
options.pro: Fast, and any worker can read it
options.con: Many workers racing for the same tickets need careful atomic claims

alternatives.pick: In memory in the owning shard, backed by a durable log.

alternatives.title: How servers are provided

options.name: Dedicated servers started on demand
options.con: A start takes tens of seconds, which players feel as waiting

options.name: A warm pool of ready servers
options.con: Costs money while idle, and has to be sized well

options.name: Player-hosted matches
options.con: Ping depends on one player's home connection, and the host can cheat or leave

alternatives.pick: A warm pool sized for the surge, with an autoscaler ahead of the daily peak.

quiz.question: A game puts every player in one queue and pairs the two who have waited longest. A player rated 1500 is often matched against one rated 2300, and the weaker players quit. What is the best change?
options: Set a fixed maximum gap of 100 rating points for every pair, and keep players waiting until another player inside that gap shows up in the queue
Sort the whole queue by rating once a minute and pair neighbours in the sorted list, so every player waits about thirty seconds on average
Split the queue into tiers at fixed rating boundaries, and only ever match players who are inside the same tier as each other
Give each player a rating and match the closest ratings, if the gap fits both windows, which widen with waiting time up to a cap
quiz.explanation: A fixed gap makes quiet hours stall, and a fixed batch delay hurts everyone equally. A window that widens with the wait trades fairness for speed in a controlled way and caps the waiting time. Hard tier boundaries leave players at an edge with few opponents and still allow big gaps inside a tier.

quiz.question: At a surge, 70 matches per second must start. Starting a new game server takes 40 seconds, and each server process runs 2 matches. The autoscaler begins adding servers only when the surge starts. About how many servers must be in the warm pool so the surge does not stall?
options: About 70 servers, which is one second of demand, since a claim on a warm server takes milliseconds
About 1,400 servers, which is 70 matches per second x 40 seconds / 2 matches per server
About 700 servers, which is ten seconds of demand at 70 matches per second with 1 match per server
About 2,800 servers, which is 70 matches per second x 40 seconds with 1 match per server
quiz.explanation: Until new servers finish starting, the pool must serve all arriving matches: 70 x 40 = 2,800 match slots, which is 1,400 servers at 2 matches each. 2,800 forgets that a server runs two matches, and 700 covers only ten of the 40 seconds. Sizing for a single second ignores the 40 second start time.

quiz.question: Matchmaker shard A owns the queue for one region through a lease. It freezes for 30 seconds in a long pause. Shard B takes the lease, rebuilds the queue from the log and forms match M1 with tickets T. Then A wakes up and forms M2 with the same tickets. What lets the allocator reject M2?
options: A fencing token issued with each lease, sent with every match, so the allocator refuses anything with an older token than B's
A check of the lease time before forming each match, so shard A declines to form a match once its own lease has expired
A much shorter lease of one second, so a paused owner loses its place almost immediately and rarely gets the chance to act
A cleanup job that finds tickets that sit in two matches and cancels the later one before the game servers start the games
quiz.explanation: A pause can strike after the lease check and before the match is sent, so the check does not close the race. A shorter lease only shrinks the window. A cleanup job runs after players have been told to join. A fencing token is checked by the receiving side, so the stale owner cannot do harm even when it does not know it is stale.
